Hey Ben,

We're getting close to contracting and the procurement team wants a tighter GPU budget estimate for the Dedicated offer. We ran a short traffic dump (attached) and tried to surface the biggest unknowns. High level:
- Current prod: ~20 req/s sustained globally.
- Campaign spikes: up to 160-200 req/s for 10-20 minute windows during promotions (weekly).
- Prompt mix: 60% short prompts (~40 tokens), 35% medium (~120 tokens), 5% long (~900 tokens).
- Avg response size: ~400 tokens typical, but heavy responses up to ~2k tokens in generative assistant flows.
- KV/cache reuse: unclear — our app opens a new session per user, but many follow-ups reuse context (we estimate 45-60% reuse).

Two asks: can you (1) translate this into a conservative GPU reserve (and a recommended burst policy) and (2) tell procurement what the expected per-token/unit cost delta vs hosted would look like?

Attached: axon_traffic_sample.csv (small dump).

Thanks,

Tom — thanks for the dump and quick summary. Looping in Marissa (pre-sales) and Rishi (solutions) to map to a sizing hypothesis. A few clarifying questions that will materially change the recommended commit:

1) Burst shape and frequency: you noted weekly promotions; roughly how often per day/week do those high spikes occur and are they synchronized across regions?
2) Latency target: is p99 end-to-end <= 200ms a hard requirement for the assistant flows or is 500ms acceptable in burst windows?
3) Session model: when a user starts a session, do you pin them to a pooled KV cache or recreate per request? Any sticky affinity currently?
4) Heavy-response patterns: what portion of the 2k-token responses are synchronous user-facing vs. async batch jobs?

If you can reply with those, we will produce: (A) a conservative GPU reserve (committed v burstable), (B) suggested GPU SKUs and oversubscription ratios, and (C) an outline of the fallback policy (model variants + routing) we recommend.

I'll draft a short mutual action list after Marissa and Rishi comment.

Adding a technical lens and an initial sizing sketch based on the sample. Notes and small asks inline.

Quick reads from the csv: session_id / request_ts / prompt_tokens / response_tokens / model_variant (local)
- Median prompt_tokens: ~48
- Median response_tokens: ~360
- 99th response_tokens: ~1,800 (rare but present)
- Average interactions per session: 2.1

Assumptions I used for sketch:
- Target p99 latency: 250ms for short/medium responses; long responses fallback to async or larger SLA (we can tier).
- Model choice: 13B opt-quantized variant for cost-sensitive live traffic; 70B for premium assistant flows (burst-only).
- Throughput per GPU (approx): 13B quantized -> sustained ~250 tok/s (conservative); 70B quantized -> sustained ~70 tok/s. These numbers change with sequence length and KV hits.

Sizing sketch (global, assume single-region primary):
- Sustained baseline (20 req/s) with avg 360 response tokens and avg 48 prompt tokens => per-request token load ~408 tokens => 20 * 408 = 8,160 tok/s. Using 13B at 250 tok/s -> ~33 GPUs sustained.
- Burst peak (200 req/s) same token mix -> 200 * 408 = 81,600 tok/s -> ~326 GPUs if all on 13B sustained. But we won't commit that many; instead:
  - Commit: 60 GPUs (dedicated reserved capacity) sized to cover typical high-day peaks + headroom with intelligent autoscale/burst to dedicated spare pool. This maps to a ~10x headroom over baseline and gives lower cost while preserving latency for most spikes with caching and request shaping.
  - Burstable floor (on-demand/dedicated spare capacity + pre-warmed instances): ability to burst to additional 200 GPUs for 10-20 minute windows (pay-as-you-go burst).

Other recommendations:
- Aggressive KV caching: with 50% reuse, effective token load drops by ~25-30%. Treat caching gains as a primary knob.
- Session pooling: pin heavy assistant sessions to 70B pools for premium users only, offload long-form generation to async workers with relaxed latency.
- Batching and prefix caching: enable continuous batching on the runtime; configure small batching thresholds for short requests to preserve p99.

Open questions for Tom (short):
- During spikes, what's acceptable tail latency for premium vs standard user tiers?
- Do you have plans to throttle or queuing UX for non-premium users?

I'll turn this into a short MU (mutual action plan) once we confirm tails and burst frequency.

— Marissa
Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Thanks Marissa — that sketch is helpful and more conservative than procurement hoped, which is good. Quick answers:
- Burst cadence: typically 3-4 spikes per week tied to marketing promotions; rarely more than one spike per day per region. Spikes are global but skewed to NA first then EU (10-30 minute lag).
- Tail tolerance: premium users need <= 300ms p99; standard users can tolerate up to 800ms during bursts.
- Long responses: roughly 8% of responses are >1k tokens and are user-facing (assistant generative flows). We cannot move those to async easily.
- Throttling: we have soft-queue UX for standard users but we prefer to avoid it for premium.

Uploading an annotated sample (column "user_tier"). Let us know if you need further fields.

Tom

Head of Product, AxonAI

Mutual action plan (next steps):
1) Redwood will deliver a two-scenario cost & capacity sheet by EOD Thursday: conservative (commit 60 GPUs + burst 200) and aggressive (commit 120 GPUs + burst 150).
2) Axon to confirm expected weekly spike windows (calendar examples) and upload final annotated traffic sample with user_tier column (you mentioned this — thanks).
3) Schedule a 45-minute calibration call (we'll bring a runtime engineer) to validate KV reuse assumptions and run a short synthetic stress test on a dev cluster.

Cost framing (very high level):
- Hosted per-token estimated delta: for your current mix, hosted API would cost ~2.5x the unit cost of a fully committed dedicated SKU at our conservative commit. But with burst and pay-as-you-go for the extra GPUs during spikes, expected blended unit cost is ~1.4-1.8x cheaper than pure hosted. We'll put exact numbers in the sheet.

Technical knobs to highlight for procurement:
- Commit size primarily buys latency predictability (lower p99) and lower baseline unit cost.
- Burst and prewarm buys availability during 10-20 min windows but is billed higher.
- Model tiering reduces required burst by redirecting heavy assistant traffic to larger but fewer GPUs.
